passage:
The first time Pooja presented Kashish's supplier analysis as her own, Kashish went home in Andheri and lay on the sofa, furious, composing speeches she would never give.
The next morning she did something duller. She opened a notes file and wrote: 3 March, supplier analysis sent to Pooja, 11:40 a.m. She started ending each week with a short progress email to the whole project group: what she had done, with the files attached.
Then she asked Pooja for coffee. "Last Thursday's supplier slides were my analysis. I'd like my name on my parts going forward." Pooja looked surprised. "I thought we were one team." "We are. I'd still like my name on my parts."
It happened once more, in April. This time Kashish took the notes file and the dated emails to her manager, and said only what had happened, in order.
The manager read them twice. "Thank you for bringing this calmly. I'll handle it."

qa.q: What did Kashish write first in the notes file?
qa.a: Kashish wrote "3 March, supplier analysis sent to Pooja, 11:40 a.m."

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling the night after the first time, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: Kashish was furious and composed angry speeches in her head, but turned that anger into careful records the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's approach work better than an angry speech?
qa.a: She kept dated records, shared progress in writing, spoke to Pooja calmly first, and only went to her manager with facts when it happened again.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen Kashish's complaint because of the way it was presented?
qa.a: The dated notes and emails, told calmly and in order, let the manager see a clear pattern instead of a personal quarrel.

grounding: Kashish keeps dated records, shares progress in writing, speaks calmly to Pooja first and takes facts to her manager when the credit-taking repeats.

passage:
"Ramesh, have you got five minutes? Just us."
"Sure, Disha. What's up?"
"In Thursday's client update, the onboarding flow was presented as yours."
"It was a team deck."
"It was. But I built the onboarding flow. Here's the document with my name and the dates, from the eighteenth to the twenty-fifth."
"...I didn't mean to take anything. I was just presenting."
"I believe that could be how it felt. But the client now thinks you designed it, and the new project was assigned to you."
"So what do you want me to do?"
"Two things. Tell the client lead that the flow was mine. And going forward, I'll present my own parts."
"That's awkward."
"A little. Less awkward than me going to our manager with this document."
Ramesh sighed. "Fine. I'll email her today and copy you."
"Thank you. That's all I needed."

qa.q: Which dates were on Disha's document?
qa.a: The dates were from the eighteenth to the twenty-fifth.

qa.q: How can you tell Disha felt calm but determined?
qa.a: Disha asked for a private chat, stuck to facts and dates, allowed that Ramesh might not have meant harm, and still clearly asked for two changes.

qa.q: What made Disha's approach a good first step before going to a manager?
qa.a: Raising it with Ramesh privately, with a dated document, gave Ramesh a chance to put it right first, while making clear that the manager was the next step.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel about emailing the client lead?
qa.a: Ramesh finds it awkward and a bit embarrassing, but agreeing to email today and copy Disha shows Ramesh sees it is fairer than the alternative.

grounding: Disha raises a credit issue calmly with Ramesh first, backed by a dated document, and asks for a correction before involving a manager.
